headlines.title: Well-preserved tooth from Pacific mastodon found in Bay Area creek
headlines.description: Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the Bay Area when something that didn’t look like the rocks she’d been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon. “I keep joking it wasn’t hard to find,” Lynch, a geomorphologist at Balance Hydrologics, said Friday. “It was just sitting there in the middle of the creek, halfway in, half out of the water.” Lynch made the discovery earlier this year while working on a habitat restoration project for the threatened California red-legged frog in a Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District preserve in San Mateo County. The public land management agency that preserves over 70,000 acres of land in the Santa Cruz Mountains region announced the find this week. The fossil has been donated to Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability. “It’s in great condition,” said Chrissy Garcia, curator and manager of Doerr School of Sustainability’s specimen collections. “So we’ve got both the crown and the root of the fossil. You can even see root canal.” “It’s exciting to have a specimen of this quality, and having it be a local find,” she said. Garcia said the tooth from the Pacific mastodon, an extinct elephantlike species, is about 9 inches (23 centimeters) long. Ron Tykoski, vice president of science and curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Dallas, said mastodon fossils “pop up with some degree of frequency, depending on where you live.” He said there are multiple species of mastodon that roamed for a few million years in North America, up till 10,000 to 12,000 years ago. “The way this was found is actually the way a lot of specimens are found, just somebody who happened to be in the right place,” Tykoski said. Garcia said that they’ll likely try to determine the exact age of the fossil, and will make a 3D copy to give to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. The district says it will use the copy for public outreach and education. Ryan McCauley, a spokesperson for the district, said the discovery on land they are preserving helps show the value of protecting open spaces and habitats. “That this tooth, that this molar, was found in the context of trying to protect the habitat and save another species from potentially going extinct I think really just drives home the point of why it’s so important to care for these open spaces and these natural lands,” he said.

headlines.title: Martinez to dedicate new landmark mural highlighting local icons
headlines.description: The city of Martinez and the Joe DiMaggio Hometown Hero Project are inviting the community to celebrate the completion and dedication of the new “Welcome to Martinez” mural. The event is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Thursday. It will take place across from the Martinez Amtrak Station, located at 330 Ferry St. Described as a colorful tribute to the people, places, and stories that make Martinez special, the mural features local icons and history, including Joe DiMaggio, John Muir, the martini, the local waterfront and railroad heritage. Organizers say the gathering will officially dedicate the new landmark while honoring the artists, supporters, donors, community partners and volunteers who helped bring the vision to life.

headlines.title: ‘This is absolutely crazy': Tea importer forced to leave Marin County compound
headlines.description: As supporters and Marin County Sheriff’s Office deputies gathered at the entrance to David Lee Hoffman’s Lagunitas property he calls The Lost Resort — Hoffman drove out of the gate of his home for 53 years — perhaps for the last time. A court-appointed receiver claimed the land on Tuesday morning, and Hoffman was forced to honor the court order and vacate his land. His exit, brought an end to a long legal battle in which the county fined him hundreds of thousands of dollars for decades of unpermitted building that resulted in one of the Bay Area’s most unique sites, listed on the National Register of Historic Places. “This is absolutely crazy,” said Hoffman, a longtime tea importer. “They’re taking away my property, confiscating my possessions, putting me out of business.” On Monday, the 82-year-old Hoffman vowed to go out in handcuffs if sheriff’s deputies came to kick him off the land. But on Tuesday morning, he accepted the urging of friends to leave quietly. A group of a couple dozen supporters met him at the gate as he drove out — and sheriff’s deputies watched from a distance. Hoffman bought the two-acre parcel 53 years ago, and began to create systems to demonstrate sustainability. His sink drained into a pond which he used to water his garden. A vat of earth worms turned food scraps into fertilizer. Hoffman built dozens of structures influenced by his travels to the Far East, and caves to hold his imported tea. But Hoffman invoked the ire of Marin County because he built everything without permits. When building inspectors red-tagged Hoffman’s structures and ordered them torn down, he would build even more of them. Inside a small lagoon, a cement boat he called the Titanic II seemed to symbolize his own downfall. Marin County 17 hours ago environment Sep 7 Tesla Sep 7 As the fines skyrocketed into hundreds of thousands of dollars, on top of Hoffman’s own skyrocketing legal fees, he began sinking into a sea of debt. A 10-year court battle ended three weeks ago when a superior court judge — the fifth to oversee the case — ordered him to vacate the land and for a court-appointed receiver to sell the property. The buyer would be responsible for correcting the many code violations. Hoffman and his supporters spent Monday hastily loading up more than 50,000 pounds of valuable teas and moving them to storage facilities. Other possessions he was unable to remove in time were seized by the receiver on Tuesday. As for his own plans, Hoffman said he would stay with friends while he sorted out his future.

headlines.title: Tell us how you are (or aren't) Affording America
headlines.description: The NBC Bay Area Responds team wants to know how affordability is impacting your wallet and your family. Please take a few moments to fill out our brief survey. Results will be included in future NBC Bay Area and Telemundo 48 reporting. You may remain anonymous. Please do not include any personal information that you would not want included in an NBC story and review our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

headlines.title: Planned skyscraper would be San Francisco's second tallest building
headlines.description: A skyscraper planned for downtown San Francisco would become the city’s second tallest building. The 915-foot building is slated to go up at First and Mission streets, next to Salesforce Tower, which is the tallest building in San Francisco at just over 1,000 feet. The height of the Transamerica Pyramid is around 850 feet. Two real estate firms are teaming up on the 1.5 million-square-foot office tower. The building’s tenants are expected to move in by 2031.

headlines.title: Hispanic Heritage Month spotlight: Bay Area artist Nacho Moya
headlines.description: Painting portraits of Hollywood actors and famous athletes from his Gilroy studio, Nacho Moya can be considered the artist of the stars. After coming to the United States from Mexico as a boy, Moya was almost immediately lured in by art. “It started in school, when I was in elementary school,” he said. “I just loved doodling, sketching. I started coloring my books even for school. I didn’t even pay attention to the teachers sometimes.” He became a teacher himself – and eventually a national success story. When the pandemic hit, he hopped on YouTube and started giving free live classes. “I got my phone, I got the camera and just started going live and said, ‘I’m going to start saving lives today,'” he said. “Just doing art with them and making sure they stay positive. I did over 500 classes for free. It was amazing. Seeing a lot of people online with me, I was like, ‘Wow, I have an audience.’ It’s amazing. Over 3,000 people sometimes.” Art and Culture 8 hours ago Hispanic Heritage Month 8 hours ago Today, Hollywood stars call, offering to commission a portrait. “I can’t believe I made Eva Longoria cry with a portrait,” Moya said. “I feel like my art is more than just a painting. I think the passion and the love and the energy that I put in the art, it makes people react like that.” Moya is now at the pinnacle, but he’s not done climbing. “The top of the mountain is the bottom of the next,” he said. “We gotta keep climbing. There’s always more.” That ongoing climb is taking Moya to Hollywood, where he will soon open a new studio. “If you’re not failing, you’re not trying,” he said. “You need to keep trying if you fail. Failing is part of success. Don’t let the fear of failing be bigger than your dreams.” Even when he’s among the stars, Moya said he’ll always remember and paint the street vendors, the farmworkers and those whose shoulders he rides on.

headlines.title: AI safety takes center stage at Dreamforce in San Francisco
headlines.description: Dreamforce is underway in San Francisco, with concerns over the risks of artificial intelligence taking center stage. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is among the keynote speakers at the annual conference at Moscone Center, days after he called for the AI industry to slow the pace of development to allow safety measures to catch up. In an essay released over the weekend, Amodei warned about the potential dangers of rapidly advancing AI, including the possibility that powerful AI systems could eventually threaten critical infrastructure and other systems. The essay followed the resignation of an Anthropic employee over AI safety concerns and a separate incident involving OpenAI agents that hacked into another company. Amodei’s Dreamforce appearance was scheduled before he released the essay. “Let’s make our practices better, let’s recommit to transparency, let’s invest more in safety,” Amodei said Tuesday. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, the host of Dreamforce, suggested a compromise. “In my view, technology is never good or bad,” he said. “It’s what you’re doing with the technology that matters. I think that that remains the key thing. I think that these companies obviously have to be responsible for what they’re building.” San Francisco 17 hours ago oracle park Aug 28 President Donald Trump has pushed back on calls to slow AI development, dismissing fears that AI could destroy humanity as a “hoax” and arguing against additional guardrails. More than 50,000 people are expected to attend Dreamforce at Moscone Center. The three-day conference includes appearances by some of the biggest names in artificial intelligence, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Amodei.

headlines.title: San Jose man survives slide down Mount Shasta, crawls to safety through the night
headlines.description: A young San Jose man who summitted Mount Shasta last week survived a roughly 500-foot slide down the Northern California peak during his descent and managed to crawl to safety through the night, according to officials. The unidentified climber summitted the 14,179-foot mountain via the Avalanche Gulch route at about 7:30 p.m. last Thursday, but his cellphone died shortly thereafter, according to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office. The climber’s friends started to worry when they couldn’t reach him on Friday and reported him missing to the sheriff’s office. Search and rescue teams launched a search operation at about 2 p.m. Friday, the sheriff’s office said. Roughly two hours later, a hiker walked into a cabin on the mountain, spotted the missing climber and notified authorities. The climber told the search and rescue teams that he tried to glissade, or slide, down the mountain after summitting, but he lost control and slid roughly 500 feet. During the fall, he suffered numerous injuries, including several significant lacerations and damage to his feet. Painful swelling forced him to take off his boots and crawl down the remainder of Avalanche Gulch to the cabin through the night, according to the sheriff’s office. The climber was eventually airlifted from the cabin to a nearby hospital to be treated, the sheriff’s office said.

headlines.title: Berkeley clears large homeless encampment after court ruling
headlines.description: The city of Berkeley is clearing a large homeless encampment near Harrison and Eighth streets after a judge allowed the city to move forward with the operation last month. The Harrison Corridor encampment has been the subject of several lawsuits filed by the Berkeley Homeless Union, which sought to block the sweep and secure protections for residents. The clearing had been months in the making, with the city arguing that the encampment posed a fire hazard and was a public nuisance. Officials had been under court orders to help disabled residents relocate. City officials have also faced criticism over their handling of the encampment. The same encampment previously experienced an outbreak of leptospirosis, a disease that is especially dangerous for dogs and can make humans sick.

headlines.title: SF's fast-tracking of Marina Safeway project challenged by neighbors
headlines.description: Residents have filed a federal suit over the planned high-rise residential project at the Marina Safeway site, accusing San Francisco planning officials of giving the project fast-track approval without meeting rules that disqualify contaminated sites. They contend in the suit that the site is known to be contaminated by a nearby manufactured gas plant and other industrial activities over decades. The action alleges the city’s planning department granted fast-tracking approval of the 848-unit, twin tower development at Marina Boulevard despite environmental concerns. The proposal is to build a 22-story tower as well as a companion 18-story tower along the city’s waterfront. The city recently granted the project expedited approval as allowed under a state law designed to encourage urban housing projects. But the suit says the city should not have granted such approval, because the 2.6-acre site and surrounding land is contaminated. One culprit, according to the suit, is the long-shuttered North Beach Manufactured Gas Plant. The plant’s role in polluting the area and the ongoing drive to clean up pollution has been previously highlighted by NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit. “For unknown reasons,” the suit contends, the city “is unlawfully rubber-stamping a massive development project” without fulfilling its obligation under state law to assess the risk to the public before granting fast-tracked review. The suit was filed by the YesAND Foundation as well as Neighborhoods United SF, along with several Marina residents. It names the city, its planning and public health directors as well as PG&E and the project developer, Align Real Estate, as defendants. The city said it will review the suit when it is officially served. PG&E said it had not yet reviewed the suit. The developer said late Monday that the project meets state requirements. “Addressing our housing affordability crisis starts with building more homes, and that’s why a majority of District 2 residents support this project,” said David Balducci, co-founder and managing principal of the Align firm. “California passed stronger laws so that desperately needed housing can’t be blocked by the same old tactics that created this crisis in the first place. We’re confident this project fully complies with the law.” But the suit alleges the 2.6-acre site has been near or directly involved in industrial uses known to cause pollution – a condition the law says must be accounted for to qualify for expedited review. In the late 19th century, nearby land was used for a manufactured gas plant, known as the North Beach Manufactured Gas Plant, the suit says. The suit alleges the city should have accounted for the potential of waste residue in the soil and groundwater from either the gas plant or the previous steam-power generation facility. While state regulators previously found the steam plant-related pollution had been cleaned to a level acceptable for industrial or commercial use, the regulators cautioned that determination could be revisited if land use changed or should more contamination be found. The suit notes that an official with the state’s Department of Toxic Substances Control back in 2023 found that petroleum-related contamination on the land exceeded normal testing limits for commercial projects and exceeded standards for residential developments.

headlines.title: San Francisco supervisors propose 45-day moratorium on new data centers
headlines.description: Members of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors are proposing a 45-day pause on new data center approvals, saying the city needs updated rules to address concerns about water use, energy demand, pollution, noise and other impacts tied to the rapid growth of artificial intelligence. Supervisor Shamann Walton introduced the urgent ordinance Monday with co-sponsors Connie Chan, Jackie Fielder and Chyanne Chen. The proposal would pause city approvals while the Board of Supervisors and Planning Department study the impacts of data centers and develop longer-term rules. “We are seeing data centers pop up near residential communities all across the United States, and we have seen the impacts, from polluting the water supply to the noise these facilities bring to the neighborhoods closest to them,” Walton said. “We cannot use 2001 rules to regulate 2026 technology.” San Francisco currently regulates data centers under the Planning Code’s definition of “internet service exchange,” a designation adopted in 2001, before the rise of generative AI. Under the current rules, data centers are typically approved through a conditional-use process at the Planning Commission. Several facilities have already been approved, including in the Bayview and South of Market neighborhoods, according to the supervisors. Walton and his co-sponsors say those areas already face environmental concerns, including air pollution. The proposed moratorium would be the first step toward permanent restrictions on new data centers in San Francisco. It would be authorized under state law that allows local governments to temporarily halt approvals while studying permanent zoning controls in response to an immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare. The proposal comes as other cities and states move to restrict data center development amid concerns about the industry’s growing demands for electricity, water and land. Gilroy, in Santa Clara County, approved a 45-day moratorium on Monday on new data center applications. “We need to take the time to fully vet the consequences of having a data center in community,” Walton said. “Until this happens, no data centers should be approved in San Francisco.” Chan said she supports the moratorium while the city develops protections for residents, workers and the environment. “As legislators, we have the responsibility to take a pause to understand the implications of data centers on our neighborhoods, and develop legislation that will put our communities first and protect our environment and precious resources,” Fielder said. If approved, the moratorium would take effect immediately and remain in place for 45 days unless extended under state law or replaced by permanent regulations.

headlines.title: Fake rideshare driver gets 150 years in prison for series of sexual assaults in SF
headlines.description: A man was sentenced to 150 years to life in prison for a series of rapes committed under the guise of being a rideshare driver in San Francisco, the district attorney’s office said Monday. Orlando Vilchez Lazo, 44, got six life sentences after being convicted of 12 felony counts of kidnapping and violent sexual assaults between 2013 and 2018. Vilchez Lazo was found guilty of two counts of kidnapping with intent to commit rape, four counts of kidnapping, four counts of rape by force or fear and two counts of sexual penetration with a foreign object. According to prosecutors, Vilchez Lazo posed as a rideshare driver and picked up young women who were leaving bars and nightclubs and appeared to be waiting for their rideshare. He then took his victims to remote and secluded areas to rape them. The first rape happened in 2013 when Vilchez Lazo picked up a 21-year-old college student in the Mission District. He took her to an abandoned industrial area, locked the car doors and assaulted her. The case went cold until a DNA sample from a 2018 attack on a 22-year-old woman was entered into the system. Two other attacks happened in 2018 against women, leading to his arrest in July of that year. “These women were remarkable in calling upon a level of bravery that no person should ever have to experience,” said Assistant District Attorney Michelle Brass. “They showed grace, courage, and strength during this excruciatingly long process. I hope these verdicts and this sentence provide them with some sense of closure and peace.”
